So what: Shows the expansion path from call handling into demand generation where proprietary external data becomes the moat — a far larger revenue opportunity per customer than contact-center replacement.
Hiring for agency and long-horizon company building 3
Melissa Tokmak says Gen Z candidates increasingly operate under a 'permanent underclass mentality' — that failing to make money within 18 months or learn everything within six months means being poor forever — which she links to an AGI-pilled belief that AI will subsume human skill sets and calls a dangerous mindset because building good things takes a very long time.
thesis🗣 Melissa Tokmakconviction: highGen ZAGINetic
So what: A labor-market read on how AGI expectations compress time horizons, predicting shorter tenures and higher churn across AI startups.
“I see especially Gen Z in these days when I'm you know looking at hiring obsessed with this permanent underclass mentality” ▶ 17:17
Netic screens for demonstrated agency plus follow-through — asking what the hardest thing a candidate has ever done was, in or outside work, then digging in on whether they sustained it rather than doing it for a weekend — explicitly avoids shiny-object seekers, and requires every engineer to visit customer sites before building product back in San Francisco.
framework🗣 Melissa Tokmakconviction: highNeticSan Francisco
So what: A transferable rubric for AI-era teams where persistence and field grounding, not tool familiarity, are the scarce inputs to correct product decisions.
“every single engineer in our company do have to go visit customers on site to build the right product back home in San Francisco” ▶ 11:30
Melissa Tokmak frames craftsmanship over signaling with a quote attributed to Martin Luther — the Christian shoemaker honors God by making the best shoe, not by putting crosses on it — and names sustaining a remarkable-people-only bar as her second northstar after the autonomous-enterprise vision, noting Palantir, SpaceX and Notion all struggled with it while scaling.
framework🗣 Melissa Tokmakconviction: highNeticPalantirSpaceXNotionMartin Luther
So what: Talent-density decay is the recognized failure mode of scaling AI companies; hiring-bar discipline and product craft over AI branding are leading indicators worth tracking in diligence.
“it says you know the Christian shoe maker, you know, doesn't honor God by putting little crosses on the shoes.” ▶ 18:29
Access, agency and the AI narrative 2
Melissa Tokmak's top non-Netic AI excitement is education, grounded in going from a small Turkish town where she didn't own a computer — messaging high-school alumni on Facebook Messenger for essay feedback — to a full Stanford scholarship; she argues AI removes resourcing and access as the binding constraints.
thesis🗣 Melissa Tokmakconviction: higheducationStanfordTurkeyFacebook Messenger
So what: Points to education as the consumer AI category she expects the most surplus from, and frames access rather than capability as the variable now being solved.
Melissa Tokmak pushes back on 'you can just go do things' optimism: removing resource constraints doesn't change that the majority of the world still won't make the choice to act, so cheaper access has a dystopian side — and she expects mainstream US AI discourse, currently very negative, to shift as first-touch use cases become help-in-crisis moments, education and understanding your own health records.
prediction🗣 Melissa Tokmakconviction: mediumeducationhealthcareAI adoption
So what: Tempers total-addressable-market math built on 'AI democratizes X' — adoption may be motivation-gated rather than access-gated — and flags help-oriented verticals as where a sentiment turn shows up first.
“It would be pretty sad if we used AI only for cost cutting.” ▶ 31:09

EconTalk · Russ Roberts 1 episode(s) · 14 insights

Dwayne Betts on the Iliad 7/20/2688 min14 insights2026-08-03
▶ Watch on YouTube
In the second EconTalk Book Club installment on Homer's Iliad, Russ Roberts and poet Reginald Dwayne Betts — both first-time readers of the Fagles translation, with Betts compressing all 24 books into three days — discuss agency under foregone conclusions, Homer's naming and simile devices, the war economy of looted armor, and the ritual function of recovering a body, closing on Betts's Freedom Reads prison-library project. The conversation is dated June 23, 2026 in the recording despite the '7/20/26' in the title, and it contains no market, macro, or asset commentary — the transferable content is framework-level, not investable.
Agency inside a foregone conclusion · 3Naming and simile as Homer's transfer mechanisms · 3War economy: armor, spoils, and revealed motives · 2Bodies, ritual, and the machinery of grief · 4Freedom Reads library model · 2
Agency inside a foregone conclusion 3
Reginald Dwayne Betts reads the Iliad as a study in constrained choice — characters who appear to have no options still keep generating real decisions — and maps it onto going to prison at 16, where incarceration felt predetermined after the crime but survival did not.
framework🗣 Reginald Dwayne Bettsconviction: highThe IliadHomerAchillesReginald Dwayne Betts
So what: A usable model for decision-making when the broad outcome looks locked in: the constraint set can be fixed while the choice set inside it is not.
“this world in which the characters seemingly have no choices, but still consistently animate what it means to make choices under the most dire constraints” ▶ 10:27
Betts identifies Zeus's near-rescue of his son Sarpedon as the poem's most surprising moment because Zeus is talked out of it by pure reason from Hera — not by prayer, extortion, or lament — showing that in Homer even omnipotence is persuadable by consistency-of-principle argument.
framework🗣 Reginald Dwayne Bettsconviction: mediumZeusHeraHomerThe Iliad
So what: Note on persuasion channels: the actor with unlimited power moved on argument, not on supplication or leverage.
“you could be all powerful and still be swayed by reason” ▶ 25:59
Russ Roberts, crediting Ido Hevroni, reframes Achilles's withdrawal as principled rather than petty: Agamemnon's seizure of Briseis replicates exactly the offense — Paris taking Menelaus's wife — that the Greeks mobilized to avenge, so Agamemnon forfeits his moral authority as commander.
causal🗣 Russ Robertsconviction: highAchillesAgamemnonParisMenelausIdo HevroniThe Iliad
So what: A clean case of legitimacy collapse: a leader who commits the offense he mobilized against loses the right to command regardless of formal authority.
Naming and simile as Homer's transfer mechanisms 3
Betts reads the poem's roughly one thousand named minor casualties as a device for showing the blast radius of war rather than for individual recognition, and links it to Yehuda Amichai's 'The Diameter of the Bomb', which he memorized in prison — a 30 cm bomb whose circle of pain widens through hospitals, a graveyard, a mourner across the sea, out to orphans' crying 'making a circle with no end and no God'.
framework🗣 Reginald Dwayne Bettsconviction: highYehuda AmichaiHomerThe Iliad
So what: A vivid framework for second- and third-order effects: the direct damage radius is trivial next to the widening circle of dependent harm.
“their names aren't there to make you know them. Their names are there to make you understand that this war has huge ramifications” ▶ 14:03
Betts credits Homer's similes with yoking the world of war to the world of ordinary work — 'the archives they held tight as a working widow holds the scales' — as the specific technical reason readers with no military experience still connect, undercutting the claim that you must share a subject's experience to engage the material.
framework🗣 Reginald Dwayne Bettsconviction: highHomerThe IliadRobert Fagles
So what: Analogy drawn from a domain the audience already lives in is the transfer mechanism for unfamiliar subject matter.
“the archives they held tight as a working widow holds the scales” ▶ 19:32
Betts reports that when his 100-line iambic-pentameter poem threaded lines from Homer, Shakespeare, and Public Enemy, a reviewer described the result as 'gritty street soaked lines' and heard no Homer at all — his conclusion is that audiences hear what they expect from a source rather than what is in it.
anecdote🗣 Reginald Dwayne Bettsconviction: highReginald Dwayne BettsHomerShakespearePublic Enemy
So what: Reception bias: framing about a source can fully suppress recognition of what the source actually contains.
“people didn't hear the Homer in it because sometimes you you choose to hear what's there” ▶ 1:09:15
War economy: armor, spoils, and revealed motives 2
Betts notes that stripping a dead enemy's armor in the Iliad is capital-equipment reuse rather than trophy-taking — most fighters are not wealthy, so they wear looted gear into the next fight, and Hector puts on Achilles's armor after killing Patroclus for protection, with poor armor a direct cause of death.
data_point🗣 Reginald Dwayne Bettsconviction: highHectorAchillesThe IliadHomer
So what: A concrete reading of a subsistence war economy where survival equipment circulates only by capture and gear quality determines who dies.
Betts argues the poem's motives invert end-to-end: characters open by talking about spoils and riches, but every dying man reverts to the family left behind, Achilles's deepest loss turns out to be a friendship rather than the woman he feuded over, and Helen repeatedly wishes she had died twenty years earlier.
thesis🗣 Reginald Dwayne Bettsconviction: highAchillesHelenThe IliadHomer
So what: Stated preferences at the launch of a costly venture diverge sharply from revealed preferences at the end — a caution about taking front-end justifications at face value.
Bodies, ritual, and the machinery of grief 4
Roberts flags that the human demand to recover a body is at least 2,800 years old and unchanged, drawing a line from Priam's plea for Hector's corpse to the sea burial of Osama bin Laden and to Middle East exchanges over the past three years where sacrifices were made for bodies as well as living hostages.
causal🗣 Russ Robertsconviction: highPriamHectorOsama bin LadenThe Iliad
So what: A persistent, non-negotiable human preference that shows up in real negotiations — bodies carry bargaining value independent of any living asset.
“this need for closure is 2,800 years old and hasn't gone away” ▶ 1:12:34
Betts's functional answer is that the body is only the entry point: it is the sequenced ritual afterward — the funeral games, the 11 days of prayer, honoring, and remembering, the careful separation of Patroclus's bones from all others — that restores wholeness and breaks the cycle of relentless weeping, and men whose lives are cut short by prison or death never acquire that template.
framework🗣 Reginald Dwayne Bettsconviction: highThe IliadAchillesPriamHector
So what: Ritual read as institutional technology for processing loss, with the physical object as trigger rather than as the good itself.
“The games were opportunities for old men to remember where they were young and the games were opportunities for young men to imagine being old again” ▶ 1:14:15
Roberts reads Achilles's refusal of Lycaon's ransom — calling the man he is about to kill 'friend' — via George Steiner's 'Errata' as an appeal to shared mortality: Achilles claims kinship because both must die, even the son of a deathless goddess.
framework🗣 Russ Robertsconviction: highAchillesGeorge SteinerThe IliadHomer
So what: The same mortality logic that licenses Achilles's mercilessness is what later makes his softening toward Priam credible rather than sentimental.
“Come, friend, you two must die. Why moan about it?” ▶ 43:07
Betts reads Priam's supplication — invoking Achilles's own aging father and admitting he wept on and kissed the hands of his son's killer — as defining a father's duty that survives the child's death, and maps it onto Randall Horton's essay about a father weeping before a judge to plead for an admittedly guilty son.
anecdote🗣 Reginald Dwayne Bettsconviction: highPriamAchillesRandall HortonRobert Hayden
So what: The plea works by separating what mercy a man deserves from the marker of guilt — the same distinction that carries clemency and sentencing arguments.
“I have wept on the feet of the man who who murdered my son” ▶ 1:00:16
Freedom Reads library model 2
Betts founded Freedom Reads on the premise of putting a million books in prison because millions of people are in prison, delivering it as handcrafted double-sided bookcases about 44 inches high holding 500 books placed on each individual cell block — so a 2,000-person prison across 20 blocks gets 20 libraries and people read in community.
data_point🗣 Reginald Dwayne Bettsconviction: highFreedom ReadsReginald Dwayne BettsThe IliadThe Odyssey
So what: A replicable unit design for an access intervention: many small libraries at the point of daily life rather than one central facility.
“I would put a million books in prison because we put millions of people in prison and I said I would do it one library at a time” ▶ 1:18:13
As evidence the model works, Betts cites Anthony Wynn, incarcerated in Virginia with a Freedom Library, who read 24 books in a book club plus roughly 40 more, and in a 15-minute interview with colleague Craig Gore spent three and a half minutes on Roberts's 'How Adam Smith Can Change Your Life' and Smith's 'Theory of Moral Sentiments' — prompting the interviewer to ask for the title himself.
data_point🗣 Reginald Dwayne Bettsconviction: highFreedom ReadsAdam SmithRuss RobertsAnthony WynnCraig Gore
So what: Demand-side proof point: measurable reading volume plus unplanned transmission of ideas between readers.
